Chapter 5

Exercise 3

Page 152
PROBLEM STATEMENT
Chapter 5, Page 152
Solution A
Step 1

(a). To determine the probability that the selected student is a management major, remember that the total number of students surveyed was 343434. Next, the number of management major surveyed was 666.

Step 2

With the number of management major and the total number of students surveyed, we simply divide 666 by 343434 to obtain the probability PPP:

P=634=0.1765\begin{aligned} P&=\frac{6}{34}\\ &=0.1765 \end{aligned}P​=346​=0.1765​

With this, the probability that the selected student is a management major is 17.65%17.65 \%17.65%.

Step 3

(b). To know what concept of probability is best suited for this problem, first remember that empirical probability can be solved by dividing the number of times an event occurs by the total number of observations.

Step 4

From the problem, we can treat the student being a management major as an event. Thus, we can say that this event occurs 666 times. Then, the number of students surveyed is the number of observations of this problem. Thus, the total number of observations is 343434.

Step 5

Given these, we use empirical probability to determine what are the chances that the event of selecting a management major will happen from a total of 343434 observations.

Solution B
Step 1

Total number of students= 343434

Number of students with a major in management= 666

a. Probability that a student is a management major\textbf{a. Probability that a student is a management major} a. Probability that a student is a management major

P(a student is a management major)=Number of students with a major in managementTotal number of students=634=0.176\begin{align*} P(\text{a student is a management major})&=\frac{\text{Number of students with a major in management}}{\text{Total number of students}}\\ &=\frac{6}{34}\\ &=0.176\\ \end{align*} P(a student is a management major)​=Total number of studentsNumber of students with a major in management​=346​=0.176​

b.\textbf{b.}b. Empirical probability is used for estimating the above probability since the probability is calculated using the information available to us.

🎯 Result

a.\textbf{a.}a. 0.1760.1760.176

b.\textbf{b.}b. Empirical Probability

Solution A
Step 1

Recall :\text{Recall :}Recall : The formula of the probability of an event is given by;

Probability of an event =Number of favorable outcomesTotal number of possible outcomes\text{Probability of an event }=\frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total number of possible outcomes}} Probability of an event =Total number of possible outcomesNumber of favorable outcomes​

Step 2

Let AAA be the first event namely "Under $1\$1$1 million" with 102102102 number of firms, BBB be the second event namely "$1\$1$1 million to $20\$20$20 million" with 616161 number of firms, and CCC be the third event namely "$20\$20$20 million or more" with 373737 number of firms.

(A.)\mathbf{(A.)}(A.) To achieve the goal of this task, apply the formula of the probability on the first event AAA.

P(A)=Number of favorable outcomesTotal number of possible outcomes=102102+61+37=102200=0.51 or 51%.\begin{aligned} P(A)&=\frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total number of possible outcomes}}\\ &=\frac{102}{102+61+37}\\ &=\frac{102}{200}\\ &=0.51 \text{ or }51\%. \end{aligned}P(A)​=Total number of possible outcomesNumber of favorable outcomes​=102+61+37102​=200102​=0.51 or 51%.​

Step 3

(B.)\mathbf{(B.)}(B.) To achieve the goal of the task, use the special rule of addition where;

P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)\begin{aligned} P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B) \end{aligned}P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)​

Step 4

First, determine the probability of the two events.

For P(B)P(B)P(B),

P(B)=61102+61+37=61200=0.305 or 30.5%.\begin{aligned} P(B)&=\frac{61}{102+61+37}\\ &=\frac{61}{200}\\ &=0.305 \text{ or }30.5\%. \end{aligned}P(B)​=102+61+3761​=20061​=0.305 or 30.5%.​

Step 5

For P(C)P(C)P(C),

P(C)=37102+61+37=37200=0.185 or 18.5%.\begin{aligned} P(C)&=\frac{37}{102+61+37}\\ &=\frac{37}{200}\\ &=0.185\text{ or }18.5\%. \end{aligned}P(C)​=102+61+3737​=20037​=0.185 or 18.5%.​

Step 6

Now, apply the special rule of addition.

P(B or C)=P(B)+P(C)=61200+37200=98200=0.49 or 49%.\begin{aligned} P(B\text{ or }C)&=P(B)+P(C)\\ &=\frac{61}{200}+\frac{37}{200}\\ &=\frac{98}{200}\\ &=0.49\text{ or }49\%. \end{aligned}P(B or C)​=P(B)+P(C)=20061​+20037​=20098​=0.49 or 49%.​

Step 2

(b) 61 of the 200 firms have $1\$1$1 million to $20\$20$20 million in income after taxes, while 37 of the 200 firms have $20\$20$20 million or more in income after taxes.

The probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes:

P($1 million to $20 million)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=61200P($20 million or more)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=37200\begin{align*} P(\text{$\$1$ million to $\$20$ million})&=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}}=\dfrac{61}{200} \\ P(\text{$\$20$ million or more})&=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}}=\dfrac{37}{200} \end{align*} P($1 million to $20 million)P($20 million or more)​=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=20061​=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=20037​​

Use the Special rule of addition\textbf{Special rule of addition}Special rule of addition for disjoint or mutually exclusive events: P(A∪B)=P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)P(A\cup B)=P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B)P(A∪B)=P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)

P($1 million to $20 million, or $20 million or more)=P($1 million to $20 million)+P($20 million or more)=61200+37200=98200=49100=0.49=49%\begin{align*} &P(\text{$\$1$ million to $\$20$ million, or $\$20$ million or more}) \\ &=P(\text{$\$1$ million to $\$20$ million})+P(\text{$\$20$ million or more}) \\ &=\frac{61}{200}+\frac{37}{200} \\ &=\frac{98}{200} \\ &=\frac{49}{100} \\ &=0.49 \\ &=49\% \end{align*} ​P($1 million to $20 million, or $20 million or more)=P($1 million to $20 million)+P($20 million or more)=20061​+20037​=20098​=10049​=0.49=49%​

🎯 Result

(a) 51100=0.51=51%\frac{51}{100}=0.51=51\%10051​=0.51=51%

(b) 49100=0.49=49%\frac{49}{100}=0.49=49\%10049​=0.49=49%, Special rule of addition

PROBLEM STATEMENT
Chapter 5, Page 158
Solution A
Step 1

In this problem, we need to determine the probability of either A or B occurring using the given probabilities.

Step 2

The given events are A and B, and we are also given the probability of event A and B. To find the probability of A or B event, we will use the formula for the probability of two events that are not mutually exclusive given in the book:

P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)P(A \cup B)=P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)

Where PPP represents the probability of each event. Event A and B is represented with a standard denotation A∩BA \cap BA∩B and the required event A or B is denoted as A∪BA \cup BA∪B.

Step 3

Probabilities given in the problem are:

Event Probability
AAA 0.20.20.2
BBB 0.30.30.3
A∪BA\cup BA∪B 0.150.150.15
Step 4

Next, we can substitute the given data in the equation to calculate the required probability of event A or B.

P(A∩B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∪B)=0.2+0.3−0.15=0.35\begin{align*} P(A \cap B)&=P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) \\[15pt] &=0.2 + 0.3 - 0.15 \\[15pt] &=\boxed{0.35} \end{align*}P(A∩B)​=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∪B)=0.2+0.3−0.15=0.35​​

The probability of event A or B occurring is 0.35.

🎯 Result

P(A∩B)=0.35P(A \cap B)=0.35 P(A∩B)=0.35

Solution B
Step 1

P(A) = 0.2 P(B) = 0.3 P(A and B) = 0.15 P(Either A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = 0.2 + 0.3 - 0.15 = 0.35

🎯 Result

0.35

Chapter 5

Exercise 31

Page 166
PROBLEM STATEMENT
Chapter 5, Page 166
Step 1

DEFINITIONS

General multiplication rule:

P(A and B)=P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B∣A)=P(B)×P(A∣B)P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B|A)=P(B)\times P(A|B) P(A and B)=P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B∣A)=P(B)×P(A∣B)

Step 2

SOLUTION

3 of the 5 people are strong leaders, which implies that the first salesperson has 3 chances out of 5 of being a strong leader and thus the first salesperson also have 3 chances out of 5 of winning the account.

The probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes:

P(First salesperson wins)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=35=0.6\begin{align*} P(\text{First salesperson wins})&=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}}=\frac{3}{5}=0.6 \end{align*}P(First salesperson wins)​=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=53​=0.6​

The second salesperson could have only won when the first salesperson was not a strong leader and the second salesperson was a strong leader. The first person has 2 chances out of 5 of not being the strong leader, while the second person then has 3 chances remaining out of 4 remaining people of being the strong leader (when the first person was not a strong leader).

Use the general multiplication rule:

P(Second salesperson wins)=P(First person is not strong and second person is strong)=P(First person is not strong)×P(Second person is strong∣First person is not strong)=25×34=620=310=0.3\begin{align*} &P(\text{Second salesperson wins}) \\ &=P(\text{First person is not strong and second person is strong}) \\ &=P(\text{First person is not strong}) \\ &\times P(\text{Second person is strong}|\text{First person is not strong}) \\ &=\frac{2}{5}\times \frac{3}{4} \\ &=\frac{6}{20} \\ &=\frac{3}{10} \\ &=0.3 \end{align*}​P(Second salesperson wins)=P(First person is not strong and second person is strong)=P(First person is not strong)×P(Second person is strong∣First person is not strong)=52​×43​=206​=103​=0.3​

Step 3

The third salesperson could have only won when the first two salespersons were not strong leaders and the third salesperson was a strong leader. The first person has 2 chances out of 5 of not being the strong leader, while the second person then has 1 chance remaining out of 4 remaining people of not being a strong leader (when the first person was not a strong leader), while the third person then has 3 chances out of 3 of being a strong leader (when the first two people were not strong leaders).

Use the general multiplication rule:

P(Third salesperson wins)=P(First two people are not strong and second person is strong)=P(First person is not strong)×P(Second person is not strong∣First person is not strong)×P(Third person is strong∣First two people are not strong)=25×14×33=660=110=0.1\begin{align*} &P(\text{Third salesperson wins}) \\ &=P(\text{First two people are not strong and second person is strong}) \\ &=P(\text{First person is not strong}) \\ &\times P(\text{Second person is not strong}|\text{First person is not strong}) \\ &\times P(\text{Third person is strong}|\text{First two people are not strong}) \\ &=\frac{2}{5}\times \frac{1}{4}\times \frac{3}{3} \\ &=\frac{6}{60} \\ &=\frac{1}{10} \\ &=0.1 \end{align*}​P(Third salesperson wins)=P(First two people are not strong and second person is strong)=P(First person is not strong)×P(Second person is not strong∣First person is not strong)×P(Third person is strong∣First two people are not strong)=52​×41​×33​=606​=101​=0.1​

We note that the probability that the third salesperson wins is much smaller than the probability that the first salesperson wins and thus the three salespeople do not have the same chance of winning the account.

🎯 Result

No, first salesperson has a 0.6 chance of winning, second salesperson has a 0.3 chance of winning, and third salesperson has a 0.1 chance of winning.

Recall :\text{Recall :}Recall : The notation n!n!n! is called nnn factorial which means the product of n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)…(1).n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\ldots(1).n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)…(1).

(A.)\mathbf{(A.)}(A.) Apply the definition of the nnn factorial to achieve the goal of the task.

n!n!=n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)…(1)n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)…(1)=40⋅39⋅38⋅37⋅36⋅35!35! Simply cancel out common factors.=40⋅39⋅38⋅37⋅361=78960960\begin{aligned} \frac{n!}{n!}&=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\ldots(1)}{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\ldots(1)}\\ &=\frac{40\cdot39\cdot38\cdot37\cdot36\cdot\cancel{35!}}{\cancel{35!}}&&\text{ Simply cancel out common factors.}\\ &= \frac{40\cdot39\cdot38\cdot37\cdot36}{1}\\ &=\boxed{78960960} \end{aligned}n!n!​​=n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)…(1)n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)…(1)​=35!40⋅39⋅38⋅37⋅36⋅35!​=140⋅39⋅38⋅37⋅36​=78960960​​​ Simply cancel out common factors.​

Step 2

(B.)\mathbf{(B.)}(B.) Recall :\text{Recall :}Recall : The permutation formula is given by

nPr=n!(n−r)!_nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!} n​Pr​=(n−r)!n!​

Now, use this formula to achieve this goal of the task.

nPr=n!(n−r)!=7!(7−4)!=7!3!=7⋅6⋅5⋅4⋅3!3!Cancel common factors.=7⋅6⋅5⋅4=840\begin{aligned} _nP_r&=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\\ &=\frac{7!}{(7-4)!}\\ &=\frac{7!}{3!}\\ &=\frac{7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot\cancel{3!}}{\cancel{3!}}&&\text{Cancel common factors.}\\ &=7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\\ &=\boxed{840} \end{aligned}n​Pr​​=(n−r)!n!​=(7−4)!7!​=3!7!​=3!7⋅6⋅5⋅4⋅3!​=7⋅6⋅5⋅4=840​​​Cancel common factors.​

Step 3

(C.)\mathbf{(C.)}(C.) Recall :\text{Recall :}Recall : the combination formula is given by

Step 2

(b) Two events are independent\textbf{independent}independent, if the probability that one event occurs in no way affects the probability of the other event occurring.

When gender and attending college are independent, then the same proportion of males and females attend college. However, 90% of the females attend college and 78% of the males attend college. Since these percentages are not the same, gender and attending college are not independent\textit{not independent}not independent.

Step 3

(c) Let the first level of the tree diagram contain the genders. This then implies that there are two vertices at the first level of the tree: Female and Male. 80% of the people are female, while 20% of the people are male.

Let the second level of the tree diagram represent college attendance. This then implies that there are two children (Attended and not attended) at the second level for each vertex at level 1. 90% of the females attend college, thus 100%−90%=10%100\%-90\%=10\%100%−90%=10% of the females do not attend college. 78% of the males attend college, thus 100%−78%=22%100\%-78\%=22\%100%−78%=22% of the males do not attend college.

Step 4

(d) Let us add all joint probabilities in the tree diagram of part (c):

0.72+0.08+0.156+0.044=1.0000.72+0.08+0.156+0.044=1.000 0.72+0.08+0.156+0.044=1.000

We note that the joint probabilities do total 1.00, because the tree diagram contains all possible outcomes.

🎯 Result

(a) 0.08=8%0.08=8\%0.08=8%

(b) Not independent

(c) See tree diagram

(d) Yes

Multiplication rule for independent events:

P(A∩B)=P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B)P(A\cap B)=P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)\times P(B) P(A∩B)=P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B)

Addition rule for disjoint or mutually exclusive events:

P(A∪B)=P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)P(A\cup B)=P(A\text{ or }B)=P(A)+P(B) P(A∪B)=P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)

SOLUTION

(a) The three contenders are equally matched, which implies that each of the contestant is equally likely to find one of the "daily doubles. Moreover, this then implies that each contender has 1 chance in 3 of finding the first daily double.

The probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes:

P(Contestant finds daily double)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=13\begin{align*} P(\text{Contestant finds daily double})&=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \end{align*}P(Contestant finds daily double)​=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=31​​

Assuming that the selection of a "daily double" does not depend on the selection of the other "daily doubles", it is appropriate to use the multiplication rule for independent events:

P(Contestant finds all daily doubles)=P(Contestant finds first daily double)×P(Contestant finds second daily double)×P(Contestant finds third daily double)=(P(Contestant finds daily double))3=(13)3=127\begin{align*} &P(\text{Contestant finds all daily doubles}) \\ &=P(\text{Contestant finds first daily double}) \\ &\times P(\text{Contestant finds second daily double}) \\ &\times P(\text{Contestant finds third daily double}) \\ &=(P(\text{Contestant finds daily double}))^3 \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3 \\ &=\frac{1}{27} \end{align*}​P(Contestant finds all daily doubles)=P(Contestant finds first daily double)×P(Contestant finds second daily double)×P(Contestant finds third daily double)=(P(Contestant finds daily double))3=(31​)3=271​​

Step 3

However, there are three contestants and all three of the contestants have a 127\frac{1}{27}271​ chance of finding all three daily doubles. Since two contestants cannot both find all three daily doubles, the events are mutually exclusive and thus it is appropriate to use the addition rule for mutually exclusive events:

P(Some contestant finds all daily doubles)=P(First contestant finds all daily doubles)+P(Second contestant finds all daily doubles)+P(Third contestant finds all daily doubles)=3P(Contestant finds all daily doubles)=3×127=19≈0.1111=11.11%\begin{align*} &P(\text{Some contestant finds all daily doubles}) \\ &=P(\text{First contestant finds all daily doubles}) \\ &+P(\text{Second contestant finds all daily doubles}) \\ &+P(\text{Third contestant finds all daily doubles}) \\ &=3P(\text{Contestant finds all daily doubles}) \\ &=3\times \frac{1}{27} \\ &=\frac{1}{9} \\ &\approx 0.1111 \\ &=11.11\% \end{align*}​P(Some contestant finds all daily doubles)=P(First contestant finds all daily doubles)+P(Second contestant finds all daily doubles)+P(Third contestant finds all daily doubles)=3P(Contestant finds all daily doubles)=3×271​=91​≈0.1111=11.11%​

(b) The three contenders are equally matched, which implies that each of the contestant is equally likely to find one of the "daily doubles. Moreover, this then implies that each contender has 1 chance in 3 of finding the first daily double.

P(Contestant finds daily double)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=13\begin{align*} P(\text{Contestant finds daily double})&=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \end{align*}P(Contestant finds daily double)​=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=31​​

Assuming that the selection of a "daily double" does not depend on the selection of the other "daily doubles", it is appropriate to use the multiplication rule for independent events:

P(Returning champion all daily doubles)=P(Contestant finds first daily double)×P(Contestant finds second daily double)×P(Contestant finds third daily double)=(P(Contestant finds daily double))3=(13)3=127≈0.0370=3.70%\begin{align*} &P(\text{Returning champion all daily doubles}) \\ &=P(\text{Contestant finds first daily double}) \\ &\times P(\text{Contestant finds second daily double}) \\ &\times P(\text{Contestant finds third daily double}) \\ &=(P(\text{Contestant finds daily double}))^3 \\ &=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3 \\ &=\frac{1}{27} \\ &\approx 0.0370 \\ &=3.70\% \end{align*}​P(Returning champion all daily doubles)=P(Contestant finds first daily double)×P(Contestant finds second daily double)×P(Contestant finds third daily double)=(P(Contestant finds daily double))3=(31​)3=271​≈0.0370=3.70%​

Step 5

(c) Some contestant will always find the first daily double, while the probability of a certain event is always equal to 1.

P(Some contestant finds first daily double)=1P(\text{Some contestant finds first daily double})=1 P(Some contestant finds first daily double)=1

After the first daily double has been selected by some contestant, there are 2 out of 3 contestants remaining that can select the second daily double (such that no contestant selects more than two daily doubles).

The probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes:

P(Other contestant finds second daily double∣Some contestant first)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=23\begin{align*} &P(\text{Other contestant finds second daily double}|\text{Some contestant first}) \\ &=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}} \\ &=\frac{2}{3} \end{align*}​P(Other contestant finds second daily double∣Some contestant first)=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=32​​

After the first two daily doubles have been selected by some contestant, there are 1 out of 3 contestants remaining that can select the third daily double (such that no contestant selects more than two daily doubles).

P(Other contestant finds third daily double∣Two contestants found first two)=# of favorable outcomes# of possible outcomes=13\begin{align*} &P(\text{Other contestant finds third daily double}|\text{Two contestants found first two}) \\ &=\dfrac{\text{\# of favorable outcomes}}{\text{\# of possible outcomes}} \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \end{align*}​P(Other contestant finds third daily double∣Two contestants found first two)=# of possible outcomes# of favorable outcomes​=31​​

2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2=28=2562\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2=2^8=256 2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2⋅2=28=256

Thus there are 256 different ways to order a hamburger and thus the advertisement is correct.

The advertisement is correct.
